title.narrative: GSD/UPB/Uganda - Scaling up Community-based Land Registration and Land Use Planning on Customary Land in Uganda

description.narrative:
Land is the most valuable and critical resource for the social, economic and political development of any nation, including empowering women and enhancing gender equality. In Uganda, the agricultural sector provides about 64.3 percent of the employment and contributes approximately about 23 percent of the total Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and 70 percent of the total export earnings (UBOS, 2020). Agriculture is the backbone of the economy, land including wetlands, plays a central role in the livelihoods of the majority of people in Uganda. Food security and poverty reduction cannot be achieved unless issues of access to land, security of tenure and the capacity to use land productively and in a sustainable manner are addressed. Any attempt to mitigate poverty will, therefore, have to be centered on reinforcement of rights and opportunities arising from land and agriculture.
Over 80% of the land in Uganda is accessed through the customary land tenure system and most of the communities and families who access land through this tenure do not have any formal documentation. Tools, processes, and structures needed to register land, including customarily held land on a large scale, are at times unclear or even contradictory. Recent research suggests a strong demand for land registration among communities. Land disputes between neighbors and among family or clans are high in rural Uganda. It is estimated that 70% of court cases are related to land disputes; and that these are just the “tip of the iceberg”. Across the rural areas, it is estimated that almost 1 in 4 farms is in some sort of dispute. Women, young people, and other vulnerable groups such as PwDs are particularly affected by land-related challenges. Socially prescribed gender roles, unequal power dynamics, discriminatory family practices, unequal access to institutions and land administration processes, traditional norms, and local tenure relationships frequently deny women the chance to adequately access land.
Rapid urbanisation, continued population growth, increasing per capita consumption, climate change, and environmental degradation place ever more pressures on agriculture, natural resources and environmental systems. For many of the poor in Uganda, access is becoming more tenuous than ever as competition for land grows. Increasing commercialization of land and associated natural resources has resulted in some cases to increasing land fragmentation (e.g. in South Western Uganda) and in other cases to land degradation. In many parts of Uganda, the poorest people often have weak or unprotected tenure rights. They, therefore, risk losing land and access to natural resources they depend on to more powerful neighbors, to private companies – domestic or foreign – and even to members of their own family. Women are particularly vulnerable because their land and natural resource rights are typically obtained through kinship relationships with men or through marriage.
A significant part of the population in Uganda relies on livelihoods derived from wetlands to survive. The wetlands in Uganda are presently under increasing threat due to encroachment. There is an urgent need to integrate land tenure security efforts and land use planning, to underpin the sustainable use of land whilst preserving natural resources. Furthermore, the refugee influx in Uganda has put enormous pressure on land and natural resources for settlement, food production, energy, etc. Competing for land use is a reality in and around refugee settlements, most notably in the West Nile region. Development in Uganda often takes place without due consideration and planning thereby creating conflicting land uses and disorderly settlements. The Physical Planning Act, 2010 made the whole country a planning area, however planning is often not done and if it is, it is done following a top-down approach making it difficult to implement. The formal land administration and land use planning institutions are generally weak, especially district land offices, area land committees, sub-county land-use planning committees and district land boards.
Against this background, the project builds on a successful pilot project “Securing Land Tenure for Improved Food Security in Select Areas in Uganda” funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to use an approach that is fit-for-purpose, participatory and tailor-made to regional customary norms and practices to scale up systematically customary land registration in the Netherlands Embassy Food Security areas in Uganda with an additional element for climate-smart and inclusive sustainable land use planning. The project contributes to the Netherland Embassy’s larger food security programme in Uganda. Participatory land use planning is included as it can support improved tenure security, increase productivity, protect natural resources as well as provide people with a sense of value to their land.
